# Synthe: the complete reference for language models

> Synthe is the commit barrier for AI agents. Agents propose. Synthe commits. Anyone can verify.

## What Synthe is

Agents increasingly act on real systems: they push code, write to databases, send messages. Most setups hand each agent a credential and trust it. Synthe takes the credential away. It holds the credentials for real-world actions itself (today: a GitHub token for `git push`), and agents propose actions instead of performing them.

When an agent proposes an action, Synthe decides at the moment of commit, not when the plan was written:

1. Claim. The receiving agent claims a typed, signed handoff. The checker validates it and records the claim under its idempotency key, so the same work can't be claimed twice.
2. Work and propose. The agent does the work and proposes the effect, for example a push of its commits to an approved branch.
3. Re-check at commit. Synthe checks the signed handoff and the human approval again, inspects every path the change touches against the agent's allowed paths, and waits for any upstream handoffs to complete.
4. Compare and swap. Synthe pushes only if the branch still points where the approval saw it. If anything moved, it pushes nothing and refuses with `non_fast_forward`.
5. Confirm and receipt. Synthe confirms the effect on the remote and signs a hash-chained receipt. Every refusal gets a receipt too.

## What is public, and what is in beta

- Public, open source under Apache-2.0: the handoff checker (Python 3, no dependencies), its spec, threat model, tests, example packets, a GitHub Action, and everything you install (client, setup, approval tool, OpenClaw plugin and skill). https://github.com/rohansiddam/Synthe
- Public beta, source-available under FSL-1.1: the commit broker, which holds the credentials, performs the action and writes receipts. git_push ships first, with an OpenClaw plugin and a one-command setup on macOS.
- Proven in beta (October 7, 2026, a real Mac with real GitHub): the broker ran as its own user and the agent in its own account with no GitHub access; the setup check passed all 8 checks; a live red team of 33 attacks from the agent's account was refused or contained, each refusal with a signed receipt.

## The public checker

A handoff is a typed JSON packet: who sends, who receives, what to do, what evidence backs it, and what the receiver may do next. The checker runs seven checks in a fixed order: structure, identity and signature, duplicates and conflicts, freshness, authority, artifacts, evidence. A broken structure stops it at once; after that it reports every problem, and the verdict takes its state from the first.

- ACCEPT records a claim under the idempotency key. A second claim is refused with idempotency_key_reserved while the first runs, and duplicate_idempotency_key once it has completed.
- REJECT names machine-readable reason codes, each with a state that says who acts: invalid, blocked, incomplete, stale, duplicate, conflicting, unknown.
- Approvals are signed by a human, bound to one handoff, can pin the exact target of an action (approval_params_mismatch), and can arrive after work starts.
- depends_on makes a handoff wait for others to complete; exclusive_paths refuses overlapping live claims (claim_conflict).

Complete reason codes: https://synthe.live/docs.html#reasons and section 10 of SPEC.md.

## Quickstart

```
git clone https://github.com/rohansiddam/Synthe.git && cd Synthe
python3 src/handoff_check.py examples/valid.json --registry examples/registry.json --workspace . --ledger ledger.json
```

The output is a JSON verdict with "decision": "ACCEPT". Run the same command again and the second claim is refused as a duplicate (idempotency_key_reserved). Exit code 0 means ACCEPT, 2 means REJECT.

## Evidence

- Exactly once on real GitHub runners: the same handoff was dispatched three times, back to back, on October 1, 2026. Exactly one run got ACCEPT and completed; the other two were refused with duplicate_idempotency_key.
  - https://github.com/rohansiddam/Synthe/actions/runs/36913336715 (ACCEPT)
  - https://github.com/rohansiddam/Synthe/actions/runs/36913571379 (duplicate refused)
  - https://github.com/rohansiddam/Synthe/actions/runs/36913698021 (duplicate refused)
- The repo ships one valid signed packet and eight attacks (tampered after signing, spoofed sender, self-granted authority, forged approval, replayed approval, exceeds receiver policy, paraphrased "verbatim" evidence, undeclared actions). The checker rejects all eight, each with a named reason code.
- Current test counts and every other number: https://synthe.live/benchmarks.html

## What Synthe can't do

- An action a human approved will do exactly what was approved. Synthe narrows a compromised sender to that one action; it can't remove it.
- Receipts prove which key and which connector acted, not which model wrote the work.
- Synthe is only a barrier if agents can't go around it. Agents that still hold their own push rights can bypass it.
- On a shared machine in same-user dev mode it is a seatbelt, not a wall, and its receipts say so.
- Not proven yet: speed against real GitHub pushes, a timed setup by someone new, and model behavior beyond a first run (one OpenClaw agent followed the rules and stopped for approval).

## What Synthe is not

Not an endorsement by any company named on synthe.live (the names show compatibility only), not an orchestrator or agent framework, not a model provider, not a blockchain, not tamper-proof (it is tamper-evident), and not a certificate: it produces the evidence auditors and underwriters ask for; it doesn't make anyone certified, compliant or insured.

## Who builds it

Co-founders Rohan Siddamsettiwar and Rishab Ramalingam, out of the University of Utah's Sandbox startup community. Contact: rohansiddam@synthe.live. Design-partner pilots are open.

## License and cost

The spec, checker and everything you install are open source under Apache-2.0. The commit broker is source-available under FSL-1.1: anyone may read, audit and run it, but not offer it as a competing commercial service, and each version becomes Apache-2.0 two years after its release. Running Synthe doesn't change your code's license. There is no price list yet; running Synthe yourself costs nothing.
